question: A team has 6 000 labeled delivery notes, but one exception type has only 40 examples. What is the sound use of synthetic data?
options: Replace all real notes with synthetic ones so the classes are balanced
Generate variations seeded from the 40 real examples, check their labels with a validator and spot checks, mark them as synthetic and add them to the real data
Generate a new eval set for the rare type with the same model and train on it too
Skip the rare type: models learn rare cases on their own
explanation: Fill a measured gap, seed from real data, filter for correctness, record provenance, and keep real data as the anchor.

question: What did research on model collapse find?
options: Synthetic data always improves models
Models collapse only when trained on images
Training recursively on generated data loses the tails of the distribution; accumulating synthetic data alongside real data avoids collapse, while replacing real data causes it
Collapse happens only with models below one billion parameters
explanation: Shumailov et al. (Nature, 2024) showed the loss of rare cases; Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) showed that keeping the real data in the mix prevents it.

question: The same model generated both the training set and the eval set for a fine-tune. Eval scores jumped from 84% to 97%. What is the main concern?
options: Eval contamination: shared phrasing and near-duplicates make the eval measure similarity to the generator, not real quality
The fine-tune is too small
97% is not high enough
The eval set has too many examples
explanation: Keep the eval set real, frozen and deduplicated against every training example, including synthetic ones.

question: Which filter is strongest for synthetic SQL examples (question plus query)?
options: Asking the generator whether it is confident
Keeping the longest queries
Removing examples with typos
Running each query against a test database and keeping only those that execute and return the expected rows
explanation: Where a verifier exists, use it: a program that checks correctness is cheaper and more reliable than a judge.

question: A fine-tune trained mostly on synthetic customer messages performs well on the eval but poorly on real messages full of typos and slang. Which risk is this?
options: Model collapse
Homogenization: synthetic text is cleaner and more uniform than real input, so the model never learned the mess
Reward hacking
Quantization error
explanation: Synthetic data tends to share phrasing and polish. Seed from real examples, vary style explicitly and always test on real data.

question: Why should each synthetic example carry provenance (generator model, prompt version, date)?
options: Training libraries refuse unlabeled data
It makes the dataset larger
So the team can find, reweight or remove synthetic examples later, for example when a generator bug or a license problem is discovered
Provenance improves accuracy directly
explanation: Datasets outlive the decisions that built them. Provenance makes them auditable and fixable, which governance (module 13) also requires.
